newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu survives no-confidence, delays decision.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu survives no-confidence, delays decision.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu defeated a parliamentary no-confidence vote on Tuesday but suffered embarrassment when 11 of his own coalition members absented themselves from the vote.
In another sign of coalition troubles, Netanyahu put off naming a new finance chief after his candidate also demanded a senior security post, complicating the appointment.

Eleven members of Netanyahu's 66-member coalition, including Foreign Minister David Levy, absented themselves from the vote. Two of the 11 could not make it to the plenum but the other nine boycotted the vote to protest Netanyahu's leadership.

"I'm very happy that the no confidence fell. I predicted as much. I told you that the government would hold," Netanyahu told reporters after his government defeated the motion by a 55-50 majority in the 120-member parliament.
Two legislators abstained in the vote which followed more than six hours of stormy debate.

Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi caused a political storm during the no-confidence debate by accusing legislator Ehud Barak, leader of the opposition Labour party and former army chief, of abandoning wounded soldiers during a 1992 training accident.
Earlier on Tuesday the prime minister's office said Netanyahu had delayed naming a finance minister after failing to come to terms on the appointment with his candidate, hardliner Ariel Sharon.

Sharon, 69, insisted Netanyahu let him join Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai and Foreign Minister David Levy in making up the Israeli leader's team of insiders who hammer out strategy in Arab-Israeli negotiations.
The post would be Sharon's first top security job since he was forced out as defence minister over a 1982 massacre of Palestinians.
"I stated (to Netanyahu) in a very clear fashion that I have to be on this team...that deals with political security issues," Sharon, of Netanyahu's Likud party, told Israel Radio.
Political analysts said the burly ex-general was sure to get the post -- a move likely to alarm the Arab world and the United States, Israel's closest ally.
"There are still problems which we will solve in the future including the appointment of ministers," Netanyahu said after the vote.

Levy and Mordechai, relative moderates in the rightist-religious government, were worried the appointment would yank the cabinet rightward at a time of rising tensions with the PLO over a three-month-old freeze in peace moves, the analysts said.

"This is something devastating for David Levy and Yitzhak Mordechai because they never wanted to share strategy and ideas with Sharon," Shimon Shiffer of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper said. "For the Americans and Palestinians, it's very scary."
Dan Meridor, Netanyahu's Likud rival, was forced out as finance minister last week in a struggle over currency reform.

Sharon's appointment would mark a stunning political comeback since he was forced to quit as defence minister in 1983 after a state inquiry found him indirectly responsible for the killing of hundreds of Palestinians by Lebanese Christians at two Beirut refugee camps encircled by Israeli troops.
The finance post would give Sharon influence in decisions on expanding Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Sharon -- nicknamed "the bulldozer" -- as housing minister in the early 1990s engineered a settlement boom that put Israel on a collision course with the United States.
